leisure

LEE-zher (first part rhymes with see) · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Free time, away from work or school, that you spend doing what you enjoy.

He spends his leisure hours building model rockets in the garage.

Example

With chores done by noon on Saturday, Marcus had a whole afternoon of leisure to fill however he pleased.

The word marks that time as truly his own: nothing required, nothing assigned, spent by his own choice. An afternoon of errands would be free of school but still not leisure.

How Strong Is It?

break → leisure → vacation

break vs. leisure

break vs. leisure: A break is lighter than leisure: a break is a short pause squeezed between tasks, while leisure is real free time that belongs to you and your own choices.

vacation vs. leisure

vacation vs. leisure: A vacation goes further than leisure: leisure is free time woven through ordinary days, but a vacation sets whole days or weeks apart from work or school entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — leisure: time you are allowed to spend as you wish

Put it together: Leisure has no smaller parts in English: the whole word is the root. It came through Old French from a Latin word meaning 'to be allowed' - leisure began as the time you were allowed to spend as you wished, and that sense of permitted free time survives today.

Use the root in a new word: leisurely: Leisure slipped into English from an Old French word for 'being allowed,' and its cousin leisurely still means done in a relaxed, no-rush way, like a leisurely walk after dinner.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Leisure is slightly formal: signs and schedules say 'leisure time' or 'leisure activities' where everyday speech would say free time. 'At your leisure' means whenever it suits you. The word always suggests time used by choice and for enjoyment, not just an empty gap in the day.
